title: Welcome Party

jokes.text: "Glad they didn't mix up your tonsillectomy with a mustachectomy."
jokes.setup: Someone signs a get-well card for Stanley who had a tonsillectomy
jokes.punchline: The joke in the card references a 'mustachectomy' — a made-up word implying Stanley's defining feature is his mustache
jokes.explanation: Solid cold open joke. The portmanteau 'mustachectomy' is clever and economical. Works as a cold open because it's immediately undercut by the reveal that Stanley doesn't have a mustache — making the card joke the setup for the bigger running bit.

jokes.text: The entire office cannot agree on or picture whether Stanley has a mustache, despite working with him for 25 years
jokes.setup: The card joke hinges on whether Stanley has a mustache — a simple factual question
jokes.punchline: Nobody can agree, Phyllis who sits across from him every day suddenly doubts herself, and a vote is called as if it's a democratic issue
jokes.explanation: This is a genuinely excellent cold open bit. The escalating absurdity — that coworkers of 25 years cannot visualize their colleague's face — lands as both a sharp observational joke about office anonymity and a perfectly structured comedic premise. Phyllis's self-doubt ('Oh, I don't know. Now I think he doesn't') is a wonderful character beat. The bit escalates logically and pays off with the elevator arrival and the frantic 'who says mustache?' vote.

jokes.text: "The whole card depends on this" — treating an absurd trivia question with boardroom-level urgency
jokes.setup: Nobody can remember Stanley's face
jokes.punchline: Jim frames the stakes of the card as if it's a crisis requiring immediate resolution
jokes.explanation: Jim's straight-man energy applied to an absurd crisis is a reliable Office formula. The line works because of how earnestly it's delivered — the card genuinely does depend on it, which makes the sincerity funny.

jokes.text: "Because we come here to do our jobs. We don't stick our noses in other people's business."
jokes.setup: Jim asks how none of them can picture Stanley's face after 25 years
jokes.punchline: Dwight — the nosiest, most intrusive person in the office — delivers this line completely earnestly
jokes.explanation: Excellent character comedy. The joke ONLY works because it's Dwight — a man who monitors coworkers, files incident reports, and has memorized everyone's medical histories — saying this with complete sincerity. The irony is rich and totally earned by years of characterization. Could easily be a fan-clipped moment.

jokes.text: "Neither of those looks like any person that has ever existed or been dreamt of in the history of human insanity."
jokes.setup: Two sketched faces of Stanley are held up for identification
jokes.punchline: Dwight's hyperbolic dismissal of both drawings as beyond the range of human imagination
jokes.explanation: The phrase 'history of human insanity' is a genuinely funny construction — escalating well past 'imagination' or 'history' into a grandiose absurdist dismissal. High quotability. The 'That said, the one on the left' kicker that immediately follows is a perfect button — he picks one anyway despite his nuclear-level rejection of both options.

jokes.text: "That said, the one on the left." — Dwight immediately picks a drawing he just called beyond human insanity
jokes.setup: Dwight declares both drawings are unlike any person ever conceived
jokes.punchline: He immediately picks one anyway, as if his prior statement has no bearing on the current decision
jokes.explanation: Perfect comedic button. The economy is exceptional — four words deliver maximum impact by completely undercutting Dwight's theatrical condemnation. The joke requires no setup beyond what just happened and lands immediately. This is tight, well-structured comedy writing.

jokes.text: "Guys, that's the elevator. What if it's him? Quick, who says mustache?"
jokes.setup: The office is mid-debate about Stanley's mustache when the elevator dings
jokes.punchline: The panic of needing to resolve a democratic vote instantly before Stanley arrives — treating it like a fire drill
jokes.explanation: Strong payoff to the cold open bit. The escalation of urgency — a simple yes/no question treated as a timed emergency — is well-executed. The physical energy of the room scrambling before Stanley walks in is a classic Office bit.

jokes.text: Stanley walks out of the elevator — he clearly has a mustache. "He does have one!"
jokes.setup: The entire cold open debate about whether Stanley has a mustache
jokes.punchline: Stanley walks out and the answer is visually confirmed — he does, in fact, have a mustache. The office cheers as if they've won something.
jokes.explanation: Excellent payoff. The cold open has been building to this moment — about two minutes of escalating absurdity — and it pays off cleanly with Stanley's visual confirmation. Stanley's complete obliviousness to why the office is momentarily electric adds a layer. The cheering as if they've won a game is a perfect touch. Well-structured, clean, visually satisfying.

jokes.text: "'Good morning, Robert,' says no one because our receptionist is in Florida."
jokes.setup: Robert walks into an empty reception desk
jokes.punchline: He narrates the absence with an unexpectedly literary/sardonic construction — 'says no one' — as if writing a novel about his own morning
jokes.explanation: Very strong character comedy. The 'says no one' construction is distinctly Robert California — he speaks in a mannered, performative way that turns mundane observations into theatrical asides. Only Robert would narrate his own entrance this way. High character integration score because this line belongs exclusively to him.

jokes.text: "Is this a video conference you're having with 'Drake featuring Swizz Beatz'?"
jokes.setup: Pam is caught listening to music on her computer at 9 AM instead of working
jokes.punchline: Robert California names the specific artist and song credit with formal precision, as if reading from a board agenda — the corporate phrasing of a casual music discovery
jokes.explanation: A top-tier Robert California joke. The comedy comes entirely from his character's verbal tic — he applies the diction of formal business communication ('video conference') to the absurd subject of listening to Drake. Saying 'Drake featuring Swizz Beatz' in full, as if reading a contract, is the punchline. High quotability and strong character integration — this is an archetypal Robert California moment.

jokes.text: "People, you should come to work already warm. 9:00 to 10:00 a.m. is the most productive potential that human beings..."
jokes.setup: Pam defends herself by saying she was 'warming up for the day'
jokes.punchline: Robert immediately pivots to a pompous management philosophy lecture that gets cut off by Nellie's arrival — the unfinished thought being funnier than any completion could be
jokes.explanation: Robert California's pomposity on display. Works because it captures his character's tendency to turn any moment into a TED talk, but gets cut off before it can become too long. The truncation by Nellie's arrival is good structure.

jokes.text: "Sorry! Sorry, everyone. I'm late, but you are all here, so no harm done at all by my lateness."
jokes.setup: Nellie arrives nearly an hour late to the office
jokes.punchline: She apologizes and then immediately absolves herself using backwards logic — 'no harm done' because everyone else showed up
jokes.explanation: Strong Nellie introduction joke. Her oblivious self-justifying logic is perfectly in character — she uses the form of an apology while actually arguing she did nothing wrong. The 'no harm done at all by my lateness' construction captures her blithely infuriating personality immediately.

jokes.text: Nellie's alarm clock snooze story: "Buzz, whack, buzz, whack" — seven times
jokes.setup: Nellie explains why she was late with a detailed timeline starting at 7:46 AM
jokes.punchline: The explanation is an eight-snooze chronicle delivered completely seriously, as if this is a reasonable justification
jokes.explanation: The 'buzz, whack' rhythm is pleasingly comic and Nellie's earnest delivery of an absurd alibi works well. The detail of counting seven times adds to the absurdity. Solid character comedy but not especially original — the 'too many snoozes' premise is familiar.

jokes.text: "No will power. That is my curse."
jokes.setup: Nellie has just described hitting snooze seven times and arriving an hour late
jokes.punchline: She delivers this as a tragic flaw — a self-aware but completely unapologetic confession
jokes.explanation: The economy is excellent — four words do a lot of work, reframing laziness as a tragic dramatic condition. The delivery as 'my curse' gives it a Shakespearean weight that's funny. Nellie treats her character flaws as ancient burdens she cannot escape.

jokes.text: "I've never believed will power was very important in a woman."
jokes.setup: Nellie calls her lack of willpower 'my curse'
jokes.punchline: Robert casually offers this as a philosophical position — a deeply sexist statement delivered with his trademark detached authority
jokes.explanation: One of the best Robert California jokes in the episode. The line is shocking but completely consistent with his character — he says the unsayable with the calm authority of someone discussing weather patterns. James Spader's delivery would make this land as horrifying and hilarious simultaneously. The joke earns its darkness through character specificity: only Robert would say this, only he would frame it as a considered philosophical belief. High character integration and exceptional economy.

jokes.text: "backwater, suburb of a suburb" — Nellie describing Scranton
jokes.setup: Nellie complains about having to move into her new apartment
jokes.punchline: She describes Scranton as a 'suburb of a suburb' — the show's own setting — with performative contempt
jokes.explanation: Meta-funny for the Office audience since the whole show is set in Scranton. Nellie's contempt for the setting the audience has spent 8 seasons loving is a good irony. The 'suburb of a suburb' construction is crisp.

jokes.text: "...and I mean no offense, but are there a lot of Irish people living around here?" — followed by the room's silent alarm
jokes.setup: Nellie is already on thin ice with the office for being rude and late
jokes.punchline: She pivots to an inexplicable, vaguely offensive question about Irish people in the area, prefaced with 'no offense' — the words that guarantee offense
jokes.explanation: Good cringe moment. The Irish question is baffling enough that the comedy is in its unexpectedness — what possible relevance could this have? The 'no offense' prefix is a comedic tell. The reactions ('Yes — Oh / No offense / None taken') show the discomfort rippling through the room.

jokes.text: "Actually, Nellie, this monologue you're delivering is very offensive. Ooh! Ay caramba! The natives are getting restless."
jokes.setup: Oscar calls out Nellie for being offensive
jokes.punchline: Nellie responds to the pushback with 'Ay caramba! The natives are getting restless' — an even more offensive phrase, delivered as if she's the wronged party
jokes.explanation: Escalating cringe excellence. Nellie being called out for offensive behavior and responding with an even more offensive phrase ('the natives are getting restless') without any awareness is perfectly written oblivious-character comedy. The 'Ay caramba' as a flustered exclamation makes it worse in the best way.

jokes.text: "I would appreciate it if you would keep that stuff on the basketball court."
jokes.setup: The office is pushing back on Nellie's comments and the tone is tense
jokes.punchline: Nellie, who is white and British, defuses what she perceives as 'ethnic hostility' by referencing the basketball court — a racially loaded and completely inapt suggestion
jokes.explanation: Sharp cringe joke. The basketball court reference — implying she associates conflict/passion with a basketball court for racial reasons — is both funny and horrifying in true Office fashion. Nellie's obliviousness makes it worse, not better, which is the point. High character integration because this perfectly captures Nellie's inadvertent offensiveness.

jokes.text: "What does that mean?" / "Or the squash court, or the supreme court. Hmm?"
jokes.setup: Oscar challenges Nellie's basketball court comment
jokes.punchline: Nellie doubles down by offering alternative courts — squash, then supreme — as if she's trying to be inclusive of different athletic preferences, completely missing the point
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation on the already-good basketball court bit. 'The squash court or the supreme court' is a great comedic escalation — Nellie pivoting through court types as if the issue is her initial court choice rather than the implication. The 'Hmm?' at the end — offering it as if she's solved the problem — is a perfect button. High quotability.

jokes.text: "I'm sorry, we're throwing a party for someone because they're being horrible?" / "I'm still not sure why this woman is even here!"
jokes.setup: Robert announces a welcome party for Nellie despite her terrible behavior that morning
jokes.punchline: Multiple office members voice the audience's exact thoughts — the absurdity of rewarding bad behavior with a party
jokes.explanation: The joke works as audience-surrogate comedy — the characters voice exactly what the audience is thinking, which provides satisfaction. But it's a functional comedy beat rather than a crafted joke. Not particularly original or character-specific.

jokes.text: Andy's talking-head: 'Two crazy kids on the journey of life / Going to Pennsylvania / On the road with my new girlfriend / But first, a small pit stop to break up with my current girlfriend'
jokes.setup: Andy is secretly going to break up with his current girlfriend to be with Erin
jokes.punchline: He narrates this with the breathless romantic enthusiasm of a road trip montage, framing the breakup as a 'small pit stop' — cheerfully callous
jokes.explanation: Strong Andy talking-head. The rhythmic poetry-like narration structure ('Two crazy kids on the journey of life') followed by the callous 'pit stop' euphemism for a breakup is very Andy Bernard. He's performing his own romantic movie while being completely oblivious to the ethical problem. Character-specific and well-structured.

jokes.text: "Oh, no, no. I meant that must be nice to have parents."
jokes.setup: Andy says the girlfriend's parents' cabin is 'a great place to let her down easy'
jokes.punchline: Erin misunderstands and clarifies she meant it's nice to have parents — a reminder that she's a foster child who grew up without them
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The misdirection is perfectly executed — we expect Erin to respond to 'let her down easy' and instead she reveals something completely unexpected and specific to her character (orphan/foster child). The joke is simultaneously funny and a little heartbreaking, which is the Office's sweet spot. Exceptional economy — the punchline is nine words. Could ONLY be Erin. High quotability because of how surprising it is.

jokes.text: The 'no kisses until the breakup is official' exchange — both characters agree this is 'important'
jokes.setup: Andy tries to kiss Erin while driving to break up with his current girlfriend
jokes.punchline: Both of them agree that 'no kisses until the breakup is official' is a principled moral stand, treating cheating-adjacent behavior with solemn ethical seriousness
jokes.explanation: Good character moment. The comedy is in the moral seriousness both characters apply to a rule that doesn't actually save them any ethical ground — they're still going to break up Jessica for Erin. The repeated 'Important. Mmm-hmm' affirmations escalate the self-delusion nicely.

jokes.text: Pam's plan to throw a deliberately bad party: "It kind of makes me want to throw a really bad party. Yeah. On purpose."
jokes.setup: The office is upset about having to throw a welcome party for the horrible Nellie
jokes.punchline: Pam articulates the passive-aggressive revenge fantasy — throw a bad party ON PURPOSE — and Meredith is immediately on board
jokes.explanation: Solid setup for the episode's B-plot. Pam's passive-aggressive scheme is well-established with 'on purpose' as the necessary clarifier that makes it funny. The conspiratorial energy between Pam and Meredith is fun.

jokes.text: "Order carrot cake" as the most subversive choice they can make for a party
jokes.setup: The team is brainstorming how to make the party as bad as possible
jokes.punchline: Carrot cake — universally disliked party cake — is offered as a weapon of passive aggression
jokes.explanation: Sharp, economic joke. Carrot cake as the ultimate passive-aggressive sabotage is funny because of its specificity and the universally shared understanding that carrot cake is the worst party cake. One of those jokes that gets a knowing laugh from anyone who has ever attended an office party.

jokes.text: Andy's worst-case scenario rehearsal: He keeps saying 'I just need you to know' and then trailing off, punching himself
jokes.setup: Andy tries to do the 'worst case scenario' practice run of the breakup speech
jokes.punchline: He falls apart immediately — can only say 'I just need you to know' before freezing, then hitting himself
jokes.explanation: Good physical comedy bit. Andy's self-directed frustration (hitting himself) combined with the verbal freeze works as character comedy. The contrast with 'consider it nailed' from 30 seconds earlier is an effective quick callback.

jokes.text: Dwight mocks Jim's Tetris skills: 'Oh, I think I'll just use this line horizontally. Oh, I have no idea what a gift this line is.'
jokes.setup: Jim says a chair won't fit through Nellie's door while moving boxes.
jokes.punchline: Dwight pivots to mocking Jim's Tetris strategy in a moving-context metaphor — 'that was one time' — with Dwight's signature contemptuous specificity.
jokes.explanation: Dwight's Tetris criticism of Jim is a recognizable dynamic — Dwight finding any angle to assert superiority. The specificity of 'using the line horizontally' (a real Tetris sin) makes it funnier to anyone who plays.

jokes.text: Nellie: "Nothing is more repellent than magicians. Bunch of grown men waving wands, pulling bunnies out of body crevices."
jokes.setup: Dwight invokes the word 'magic' in reference to moving the chair
jokes.punchline: Nellie delivers an unprompted and viscerally specific anti-magician rant — 'body crevices' being the key escalation
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke with exceptional quotability. 'Pulling bunnies out of body crevices' is a brilliantly specific and disgusting escalation of the standard rabbit-from-hat trick — the word 'crevices' doing enormous comedic work. The intensity of Nellie's hatred for magicians ('repellent') feels pathological and specific, which sets up the reveal of her ex-boyfriend being a magician perfectly (though we don't know that yet). This line will land differently on rewatch, making it especially rewatchable.

jokes.text: Jim on the phone: "hauling cube" — 'That's moving boxes. We just came up with the term to make it sound cooler.'
jokes.setup: Jim calls Pam from Nellie's apartment
jokes.punchline: He's invented office jargon for the embarrassing task of carrying boxes to make it sound like professional work
jokes.explanation: Strong Jim joke. The immediate explanation undercuts the cool term completely and honestly — 'to make it sound cooler' is pure self-aware Jim. Very quotable and characterful. Could be clipped as a standalone Jim bit.

jokes.text: Pam's suggestion to 'hire a magician' — Pam says it as a joke, but Jim immediately says 'What? Trust me. Okay.'
jokes.setup: Pam's prank party planning — 'hire a magician' is said half-jokingly
jokes.punchline: Jim immediately endorses it with mysterious authority, knowing about Nellie's magician ex but not being able to explain why
jokes.explanation: Good structural joke that works on two levels — as a comedy beat and as a plot engine. Jim's 'Trust me. Okay.' delivered with confident authority while Pam (and the audience) doesn't know why is well-executed. The reversal — Jim usually being the anti-prank party member who suddenly endorses the worst possible idea — creates good dramatic irony.

jokes.text: Andy at the bachelorette party explaining Erin: "Why is Erin with me? That's a great question. She is my co-worker and she needed a ride because she totaled her car."
jokes.setup: Andy shows up to break up with his girlfriend and she's surrounded by her friends at what turns out to be her bachelorette party
jokes.punchline: He preemptively addresses the elephant in the room with a scripted excuse — 'she totaled her car' — that sounds completely fabricated
jokes.explanation: Solid cringe setup. Andy's cover story is transparently bad, which is the point. The 'That's a great question' opener — responding to his own internal monologue — is a nice touch.

jokes.text: "Okay, Andy, that is a bachelorette party. This is Jessica's friends and they've been drinking during the daytime." — followed by 'Should we go? / Yeah'
jokes.setup: Andy and Erin realize they've walked into a bachelorette party full of Jessica's friends
jokes.punchline: Erin's matter-of-fact assessment of the situation ('they've been drinking during the daytime') followed by their brief consideration of leaving — and then immediately deciding to do it anyway
jokes.explanation: Good cringe setup. 'They've been drinking during the daytime' as a threat assessment is funny. The immediate pivot from 'should we go?' to staying anyway is classic cringe comedy — acknowledging the exit and refusing it.

jokes.text: Andy and Erin looking at photos of Jessica's new boyfriend — Andy keeps misidentifying the relationship: 'I'm guessing he's some kind of close romantic friend. Like a boyfriend? You read my mind.'
jokes.setup: Andy is looking at photos of Jessica with another man while at her bachelorette party
jokes.punchline: He repeatedly refuses to use the word 'boyfriend,' substituting absurd euphemisms — 'some kind of close romantic friend' — then immediately admits Erin's correction is correct
jokes.explanation: Strong character beat. Andy's progressive reluctance to admit the obvious — his girlfriend has been dating someone else — played through increasingly ridiculous euphemisms is well-executed. 'You read my mind' is a nice dry punchline. Shows Andy's oblivious self-protection.

jokes.text: "Whoa. Here's one with his face whited out. Maybe someone threw a pie in his face. New theory, he's a hated Italian politician."
jokes.setup: They find a photo where the boyfriend's face has been scribbled out
jokes.punchline: Andy generates increasingly specific and absurd theories for why someone's face might be whited out — pie, Italian politician — before Erin supplies the obvious answer
jokes.explanation: Good absurdist riff. The 'hated Italian politician' theory is a left-field escalation that works well. Andy's manic theory-generation as a defense mechanism against the obvious truth is strong character comedy.

jokes.text: "That's what I call my box full of photos of Henry. Why not call...Shh."
jokes.setup: Jim and Dwight are caught snooping through a box labeled 'Benjamin'
jokes.punchline: Nellie reveals 'Benjamin' is what she names her box of ex-boyfriend photos — Jim starts to question the logic and is immediately shushed
jokes.explanation: Solid joke. The non-sequitur naming convention (why 'Benjamin'?) is funny, and Jim's attempted logic question being cut off preserves the absurdity — asking 'why not call it...' doesn't need an answer because the answer doesn't matter. The shush is the punchline.

jokes.text: "What kind of restaurant?" — Dwight's single-track question after learning Nellie's ex left her for a waitress
jokes.setup: Nellie tearfully reveals her ex ran off with a waitress at their favorite restaurant
jokes.punchline: Dwight's only question is about the type of restaurant — practically ignoring the emotional content entirely
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Maximum economy — three words — and maximum character specificity. Only Dwight would respond to a tearful breakup story by asking about the restaurant category. It's not even malicious; he genuinely finds this to be the relevant data point. Perfect character integration. Very high quotability — the kind of line fans repeat. Comparable to anchor-level economy.

jokes.text: "Ah, but what's 10 years of bliss down the drain compared with the thrill of starting over with nothing and no one?"
jokes.setup: Nellie describes having to sell her flat at a loss after the breakup
jokes.punchline: She delivers this devastatingly self-pitying question with the cadence and irony of a toast — the 'thrill of starting over with nothing and no one' is a perfect darkly comic inversion
jokes.explanation: Excellent line. 'What's 10 years of bliss down the drain compared with the thrill of starting over with nothing and no one?' is written with the acid wit of someone who uses language as self-protection. The phrase 'starting over with nothing and no one' is surprisingly moving and funny simultaneously — peak Office comedy. Very quotable. Nellie's dark self-deprecating humor works wonderfully here and makes her sympathetic.

jokes.text: Jim: 'I'm so sorry. These must be very painful memories. If it would help you to forget, [Dwight grabs candlestick] in the brain stem with this candlestick.'
jokes.setup: Jim offers sincere condolences to Nellie about her painful memories
jokes.punchline: Dwight has already picked up a candlestick and is ready to physically erase the memories by hitting her — Jim finishes the sentence Dwight has already begun
jokes.explanation: Strong Dwight joke. The visual of Dwight already having the candlestick ready — anticipating this offer before Jim finishes the sentence — is perfectly absurd. Jim finishing the sentence as if presenting a legitimate medical option is excellent. The clinical 'in the brain stem' makes it funnier and more specific.

jokes.text: Jim looks at Nellie's photo collection: 'Just one quick question — was this Halloween or—?' 'God, no.'
jokes.setup: Jim and Dwight have discovered Nellie's box of photos of her ex-boyfriend
jokes.punchline: Jim delicately asks if the photos were from Halloween — implying the ex-boyfriend was in some kind of costume or makeup — and Nellie's 'God, no' confirms the photos are genuinely how he looked all the time
jokes.explanation: Good visual joke. The question implies something deeply strange about the ex-boyfriend's appearance — a magician, as we'll learn — and Nellie's horrified 'God, no' combined with 'That's the most embarrassing thing of all of this' sets up the reveal perfectly. Works as both a standalone joke and dramatic irony setup.

jokes.text: "What kind of fool gets her heart broken by a bloody stage magician?"
jokes.setup: Jim's question about Halloween reveals the ex-boyfriend was a magician — the reason for Nellie's anti-magician rant earlier
jokes.punchline: Nellie reveals the twist and immediately self-flagellates with 'what kind of fool' — calling herself a fool is both the payoff and a Nellie-specific response
jokes.explanation: The episode's best joke. The reveal that Nellie's visceral hatred of magicians ('repellent,' 'body crevices') was personal all along — she dated one who broke her heart — is a perfectly planted and paid-off comedy twist. The line 'What kind of fool gets her heart broken by a bloody stage magician?' is self-aware, darkly funny, and completely consistent with Nellie's character. The 'bloody stage magician' phrasing is British and specific. This is excellent comedy writing: the callback rewards attention and retroactively improves the earlier joke. Structural score is high because of the perfect callback architecture.

jokes.text: Jim on the phone urgently telling Pam to cancel the magician: 'Call it off, Pam. Call it off... Cancel the magician. Trust me.'
jokes.setup: Jim now knows Nellie's ex was a magician and that Pam has hired a magician for the party
jokes.punchline: Jim's frantic whispered phone call — 'call it off' — spoken with the urgency of defusing a bomb, while Dwight is standing nearby
jokes.explanation: Solid structural beat. The irony of Jim having recommended the magician and now frantically trying to cancel it is well-played. The urgency of the whispered 'call it off' is funny given the context.

jokes.text: Jim calls off the prank party on the phone with Pam, who thinks it was her idea to go normal. Jim: 'Call it off, Pam. Call it off, okay? Cancel the magician. Trust me.'
jokes.setup: Jim now knows Nellie's ex was a magician — he urgently needs to cancel the hired magician from the bad party.
jokes.punchline: Jim tells Pam to cancel the magician without explaining why — the audience understands the irony of accidentally booking Nellie's specific trauma as party entertainment.
jokes.explanation: The comedy here is in the dramatic irony — we know why, Pam doesn't, and Jim can't explain without exposing Nellie's secret. Functional plot-comedy.

jokes.text: Pam: 'Like, not mean. Just a regular party. Not mean.' — Phyllis: 'I knew she'd crack. I wanted to leave you out, you know.'
jokes.setup: Pam tries to convince the party committee to go normal and nice
jokes.punchline: Phyllis immediately calls her out for cracking and adds she wanted to exclude Pam from the start — Phyllis's uncharacteristic ruthlessness is the joke
jokes.explanation: Funny character subversion. Phyllis — usually the sweet one — being the most committed to the mean party plan and criticizing Pam for backing down is a nice reversal. 'I wanted to leave you out, you know' is delivered as a gentle complaint, which makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Meredith: 'Toots, we're not stopping this train, so get off the tracks.' / 'Suck it.'
jokes.setup: Pam tries to call off the mean party plan
jokes.punchline: Meredith delivers two separate blunt dismissals — first a folksy metaphor, then a flat 'Suck it' — both completely committed
jokes.explanation: 'Suck it' as a flat, cheerful dismissal after a folksy train metaphor is very Meredith — maximally direct with zero social grace. The two-beat combo (metaphor then blunt profanity) works well. High economy score.

jokes.text: Andy is offered a gummy penis and asks for 'just some gummy bears.' Lauren: 'These are delicious.' Andy: 'But they're penises.' Lauren: 'And we come to Matthew...'
jokes.setup: Andy is at a bachelorette party, completely out of place, trying to maintain normalcy.
jokes.punchline: The gummy penis exchange — Andy's preference for regular gummy bears being met with 'these are delicious / but they're penises / and we come to Matthew' — captures the chaos of the bachelorette party swallowing Andy whole.
jokes.explanation: Standard bachelorette party comedy. Functional cringe/visual gag but not particularly inventive. The pivot to 'Matthew' saves it from being entirely generic.

jokes.text: Andy at the bachelorette party: 'Do you want a gummy penis? / No. I'll just have some gummy bears. / These are delicious. / But they're penises.'
jokes.setup: Andy is stuck at his girlfriend's bachelorette party trying to act natural
jokes.punchline: Andy eats gummy bears that are actually gummy penises, finds them delicious, and has to be informed of what he's eating
jokes.explanation: Reliable bachelorette party gag elevated by Andy's specific obliviousness. 'These are delicious / But they're penises' is a clean setup-punchline with good economy. The joke is familiar terrain but executed well in context.

jokes.text: "Maybe we don't pop that one. / No. Pop it. Pop it. Pop it."
jokes.setup: The group is popping balloons at the bachelorette party
jokes.punchline: Andy tries to exempt one balloon, presumably aware of what's inside — the friends insist on popping it anyway with escalating enthusiasm
jokes.explanation: Functional cringe beat. The escalating chant of 'Pop it' against Andy's protest is good party energy, though the visual gag of what's inside the balloon doesn't come through in transcript form.

jokes.text: Andy's old friend at the party: "You are one of the good ones, Nard Dog." — women asking Andy to sing
jokes.setup: Andy is at his girlfriend's bachelorette party while planning to break up with her for another woman
jokes.punchline: He's praised as 'one of the good ones' by her friend — the irony being that he's literally there on false pretenses to end the relationship
jokes.explanation: Good dramatic irony. 'One of the good ones' at this specific moment is a well-placed ironic compliment that the audience appreciates more than Andy deserves.

jokes.text: Andy pressed into singing at the bachelorette party: 'Well, you guys are doing a pretty good job with the scary yelling, so—' then is forced to sing 'Loch Lomond'
jokes.setup: The bachelorette party crowd wants Andy to sing despite the increasingly awkward situation
jokes.punchline: He tries to deflect ('scary yelling') and is then forced to perform a mournful Scottish ballad at a bachelorette party
jokes.explanation: Good cringe comedy. Andy being forced to perform while planning a breakup is absurdly uncomfortable. 'By yon bonnie banks' at a bachelorette party is perfectly wrong-footed. The 'scary yelling' line is a funny understated description of bachelorette party energy.

jokes.text: Party committee discussing code names: 'Ryan was "Douche Bag."' / 'Hey, that's not a code name. That's just an insult. Plus, everyone would know who you meant.'
jokes.setup: The office discusses using code names to talk about Nellie without her knowing
jokes.punchline: Ryan's 'code name' was 'Douche Bag' — which Oscar correctly identifies as not a code name at all, just an insult that everyone would recognize
jokes.explanation: Sharp joke. Oscar's logical dissection — 'that's not a code name, that's just an insult, plus everyone would know who you meant' — is perfectly structured. The two separate objections landing in sequence ('it's an insult' AND 'it would defeat the purpose of a code') make it funnier than one objection alone. Ryan-specific humor that lands without Ryan being present.

jokes.text: "How about 'Pam'? Simple, easy to remember." / "Because there's someone already here named Pam."
jokes.setup: The group is brainstorming code names for Nellie
jokes.punchline: Kevin suggests 'Pam' as a code name — a real person's name who is present — and Oscar has to point out the obvious flaw
jokes.explanation: Excellent Kevin joke. The simplicity and sincerity of Kevin suggesting 'Pam' — already a name in use in this very office — and framing it as the ideal solution ('simple, easy to remember') is wonderful. Only Kevin would do this. Oscar's deadpan explanation of why it's wrong is the perfect straight-man button. High economy: the whole joke is about 12 words.

jokes.text: The musician hired for Nellie's party: "They asked me to play only originals. I said, 'Have you heard my originals? They're terrible.' They said, 'Even better.' I said, 'I get it. It's an ironic party for Nellie.'"
jokes.setup: A musician is playing at the party — it becomes clear the party is intentionally bad
jokes.punchline: The musician has figured out the meta-joke of the party and has accepted his role in it, cheerfully narrating the conspiracy
jokes.explanation: Good meta-moment. The musician's self-aware description of the scheme is funny — he's in on it and comfortable with the fact that his originals are 'terrible.' 'I get it. It's an ironic party for Nellie' is a good deadpan line. The comic timing of this being delivered straight to the camera (presumably) works well.

jokes.text: The musician announces his song will be 'over a half-hour long.'
jokes.setup: The deliberately bad party has a musician playing originals.
jokes.punchline: He announces his opening song is 'over a half-hour long' — the single detail that crystalizes how bad this party is.
jokes.explanation: Maximum economy — 'this first song's over a half-hour long' does everything needed in one sentence. It defines the deliberate badness of the party in the most concrete terms. Simple and effective.

jokes.text: Kenny at the party: 'You invited me to go shopping with you / I like hanging out with you. You're a cool guy. / Which proves my point that I'm gay.'
jokes.setup: Andy claims to be gay; his friend Kenny disputes this based on prior behavior
jokes.punchline: Andy seizes on Kenny's evidence of friendship as proof of his claimed gayness — 'which proves my point' — using completely backwards logic
jokes.explanation: Sharp comedic logic inversion. Andy taking friendly social behavior as evidence for his fabricated sexual orientation — and Kenny's confused reaction — works well. 'Which proves my point that I'm gay' is a confident non-sequitur delivered perfectly in character.

jokes.text: Jessica: 'Andy, you're not gay. And you seemed pretty excitable.' / 'Well, I was faking it. I had to fake it every time.'
jokes.setup: Jessica challenges Andy's claim to be gay based on their relationship
jokes.punchline: Andy doubles down and claims to have faked everything, inverting the cultural cliché (women faking it) in a committed but absurd way
jokes.explanation: The cliché inversion (Andy claiming to have faked excitement) is a sharp bit. 'I had to fake it every time' delivered with wounded dignity works as an escalation of his desperate lie.

jokes.text: "with John Stamos" — Andy uses John Stamos as evidence of what actually excites him
jokes.setup: Andy is trying to prove he's gay to get out of the relationship
jokes.punchline: He invokes John Stamos as the person he's actually attracted to — a completely random and specific celebrity choice that reveals more about Andy than intended
jokes.explanation: Excellent celebrity-specific joke. The choice of John Stamos is perfectly Andy — vaguely Full House adjacent, a very 'Andy Bernard' kind of celebrity crush whether real or invented. The specificity of the name is what elevates this above a generic 'male celebrity' joke. High quotability because of how committed and specific it is.

jokes.text: Robert California's toast: 'Pam, on the other hand, is a most unwelcome, entitled and unfriendly presence in our company.'
jokes.setup: Robert delivers a toast welcoming Nellie to the company
jokes.punchline: He pivots immediately from welcoming Nellie to publicly roasting Pam with the same formal structure — 'on the other hand' — as if this is a natural part of a toast
jokes.explanation: Outstanding Robert California joke. The perfect parallelism — welcoming Nellie in formal toast language, then immediately using the same language to denounce Pam — is brilliant. Only Robert would think a workplace toast is an appropriate venue for singling out another employee for public condemnation. The 'on the other hand' pivot is the comedic engine. Very high character integration and quotability.

jokes.text: "Every day, I imagine how happy I'd be if Pam died."
jokes.setup: Robert's toast has opened the floor to anti-Pam sentiment; Nellie responds to the question of what she thinks of Pam
jokes.punchline: Nellie casually delivers what should be a horrifying confession — fantasizing about Pam's death daily — in a conversational tone
jokes.explanation: Strong dark comedy from Nellie. The flat delivery of 'I imagine how happy I'd be if Pam died' — phrased not as a threat but as a daily meditation — is maximally dark and very funny. The specificity of 'every day' makes it worse in the best way. High economy: ten words for a genuinely shocking laugh.

jokes.text: Jim defends Pam at the toast with increasingly damning faint praise: 'she is misunderstood...maybe there's some stuff in her past that's a little messed up and probably makes her such a torture to work with.'
jokes.setup: Jim tries to defend Pam against Robert and Nellie's condemnation
jokes.punchline: His defense gradually collapses into inadvertent insults — 'a torture to work with' — as he tries harder to be generous
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalating joke. The gradual degradation of Jim's defense — from 'she is misunderstood' through 'maybe there's stuff in her past' to 'makes her such a torture to work with' — is a beautifully constructed descent into backhanded compliment territory. Jim's increasing verbal flailing as he tries to help is very character-specific. The rhythm of the qualifiers ('only a little bit, enough, a good amount, not the most') is a subtle but funny beat.

jokes.text: The office chanting 'We hate Pam! We hate Pam!' in unison
jokes.setup: Robert leads the office in expressing anti-Pam sentiment
jokes.punchline: The office breaks into a unanimous chant — 'We hate Pam' — like a sports crowd, with everyone fully committed
jokes.explanation: Good escalation payoff. The chant emerging organically from Robert's formal toast is a great structural beat — the formality of the occasion crashing into mob psychology. Works as an ensemble visual that's funny in its absurd intensity.

jokes.text: Robert: 'Do you ever wish she would just disappear?' — the camera cuts to Pam presumably watching from outside
jokes.setup: Robert has led the office in publicly denouncing Pam, escalating to asking if they wish she'd disappear
jokes.punchline: Inferred: Pam is watching or overhearing this — the camera likely cuts to her horrified reaction
jokes.explanation: Strong cringe beat that works as the peak of the anti-Pam sequence. Robert's question escalates the mob dynamic while presumably the camera shows Pam's reaction. Works as sustained cringe payoff.

jokes.text: Jim and Erin's post-bachelorette debriefing: 'That was a really rough scene.' / 'Right? Rough scene. Yeah.'
jokes.setup: Andy and Erin have just survived the bachelorette party disaster
jokes.punchline: They bond over the horror of it with comic understatement — 'rough scene' — as if reviewing a performance
jokes.explanation: Functional comedic exhale after the cringe set piece. 'Rough scene' as shared understatement is sweet and mildly funny but not a particularly crafted joke — more of a character moment between Andy and Erin.

jokes.text: 'At least we can kiss now.' / 'Oh, yeah.'
jokes.setup: They've just been through a disaster at the bachelorette party; Andy finally broke up with Jessica
jokes.punchline: The silver lining Andy identifies is simply 'we can kiss now' — the moral stand from earlier (no kissing until the breakup is official) now fulfilled
jokes.explanation: Sweet callback to their principled no-kissing rule. Works as a quiet comedic payoff to the 'important' moral stand they took earlier. The contrast between the disaster they just caused and the simple reward they're celebrating is funny in its smallness.

jokes.text: Andy: 'You know, that stuff that I said about you to her, that's just... I was dating her at the time.'
jokes.setup: Erin and Andy share a moment; Andy references something bad he apparently said about Erin to Jessica
jokes.punchline: His explanation — 'I was dating her at the time' — is offered as if that fully explains and excuses having said terrible things
jokes.explanation: Good cringe beat. Andy's attempt at an apology that isn't quite an apology — citing the context of his prior relationship as full mitigation — is character-specific. The 'Yeah...Ugh...Yeah' rhythm of their mutual discomfort is honest and funny.

jokes.text: Andy/Erin nausea: 'Probably from seeing that turkey. / Oh yeah. When we drove by the farm. Always does that.'
jokes.setup: One of them (presumably Erin) is feeling queasy after the bachelorette party
jokes.punchline: The cause is identified as having driven by a turkey farm — a specific, mundane rural experience that Erin apparently has a documented history with
jokes.explanation: 'Always does that' implies this is a recurring Erin problem — she reliably gets nauseated by turkey farms. This small detail is funny in its specificity and ordinariness. The word 'always' does the comedic work.

jokes.text: The magician arrives at the party: 'Are you Nellie? I think you're my volunteer.' / Dwight intercepts: 'No, I'll do it. I will volunteer.'
jokes.setup: The party magician is about to engage Nellie — which Jim and Dwight know would be catastrophic given her history
jokes.punchline: Dwight immediately throws himself in front of the situation to be the volunteer, protecting Nellie without being able to explain why
jokes.explanation: Good structural beat. Dwight's immediate self-sacrifice to protect Nellie from the magician she hates — while having to hide his reason — is a good cringe-comedy setup. Works well as the beginning of the magician sequence payoff.

jokes.text: The magician to Dwight: 'Oh, big guy, huh? How's the air up there? Watch out for birds.'
jokes.setup: Dwight volunteers to be the magician's assistant
jokes.punchline: The magician immediately starts in with hacky tall-person material at Dwight, who is not even particularly tall
jokes.explanation: The joke here is that the magician is bad — his crowd work is hacky. 'Watch out for birds' is intentionally a terrible joke, which is part of the meta-point. Scores low on craft because the comedy is about the magician being bad, not about the joke itself being good. This is intentional badness, which is slightly different from a weak joke.

jokes.text: Dwight's sabotage: blurts out 'It's the four of hearts' before looking at the card; magician responds 'No hablo el cardo, señor?'
jokes.setup: The magician is doing a card trick and tells Dwight not to say what the card is
jokes.punchline: Dwight announces the card value immediately, sabotaging the trick; the magician responds with a baffling fake-Spanish non-sequitur as if Dwight is foreign
jokes.explanation: Good slapstick beat. Dwight's inability to follow the magician's one instruction is funny. 'No hablo el cardo' is a nonsense Spanish phrase ('I don't speak the card') that the magician uses to save face — terrible crowd work that makes the magician funnier as an incompetent character.

jokes.text: Jim explains his sabotage credibility: 'Little known fact about me — before I was a magician, I worked at a rope factory. Not true, because that's not a real place.'
jokes.setup: Jim uses a fake backstory to undermine the magician's rope trick
jokes.punchline: He or Dwight immediately debunks it — 'Not true, because that's not a real place' — the self-refutation within the same beat
jokes.explanation: Solid absurdist bit. The immediate self-correction — 'not true, because that's not a real place' — is a funny meta beat. The specific detail 'rope factory' as the chosen fake workplace is amusing in its obscurity.

jokes.text: Dwight deliberately destroys the magician's card shuffling by violently smashing the deck — magician: 'You didn't just do that on purpose, did you?'
jokes.setup: The magician asks Dwight to shuffle the deck.
jokes.punchline: Dwight apparently destroys the shuffle in a dramatic way — the magician's indignant 'You didn't just do that on purpose, did you?' implies a spectacular act of deliberate sabotage.
jokes.explanation: Good Dwight physical comedy beat — Dwight sabotaging a magician's trick by brute force is very on-brand. The visual gag is inferred from the magician's reaction line.

jokes.text: "Okay, scram, wizard."
jokes.setup: The magician complains his show is being sabotaged
jokes.punchline: Dwight dismisses him with 'scram, wizard' — using 'wizard' as a demeaning synonym for 'magician'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout lines. 'Scram, wizard' is exactly two words and delivers maximum impact — it's dismissive, slightly medieval, and deeply Dwight. The choice of 'wizard' instead of 'magician' implies Dwight considers them the same category of contemptible practitioner. Very high quotability — this is the kind of line that gets clipped and shared. Perfect economy: no word could be added or removed.

jokes.text: Nellie's unexpected defense: 'I thought it was quite fun. In fact, I think they're brilliant employees in their own way.'
jokes.setup: Jim apologizes for the party going wrong as a prank; we expect Nellie to be offended
jokes.punchline: Nellie — who hates magicians with documented passion — found the magician being humiliated to be delightful, and interprets the whole thing as a sincere good-faith effort
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural payoff. The bad party actually worked perfectly for Nellie because the magician abuse was cathartic given her past. The misdirection is well-earned: we expect her to be offended, but her specific trauma makes this the ideal party. Robert California's confusion about why it's a 'great party' adds a layer.

jokes.text: Kevin's complaint: "This cake has vegetables in it like a salad bar, Robert."
jokes.setup: Robert declares the party was great; Kevin registers his one complaint
jokes.punchline: Kevin's issue with the carrot cake is framed as a factual consumer complaint — it has vegetables 'like a salad bar'
jokes.explanation: Excellent Kevin callback. 'This cake has vegetables in it like a salad bar' is a perfect Kevin observation — he can't quite articulate what's wrong with carrot cake but identifies it as a health food infiltrator. The 'Robert' at the end, addressed as if filing a formal complaint with management, is the perfect button. Very high quotability and strong character integration — only Kevin would frame this as a salad bar issue.

jokes.text: "How do I get this taste out of my mouth?"
jokes.setup: Kevin has just established that carrot cake is unacceptable
jokes.punchline: He's already eaten enough of the carrot cake to need to neutralize the taste — while continuing to complain about it
jokes.explanation: Good Kevin button joke. The implication that he kept eating despite his complaints is very Kevin. Short and character-specific.

jokes.text: Andy returns to Jessica's party: "Super duper honesty time. I'm not gay. In fact, I'm so not gay that I'm in love with a girl."
jokes.setup: Andy previously claimed to be gay to break up with Jessica
jokes.punchline: He escalates the honesty framing ('super duper') to retract his lie and immediately declares love for Erin
jokes.explanation: Good callback payoff. 'Super duper honesty time' escalating from 'super honesty time' is a nice structural touch. 'So not gay that I'm in love with a girl' is well-constructed and has Andy's specific earnest quality. Works as both a callback and a declaration-of-love scene.

jokes.text: "Total relationship material." — Andy using Nellie's/Jessica's earlier dismissal of Erin as a declaration of love
jokes.setup: Jessica had told Andy that Erin 'wasn't relationship material'
jokes.punchline: Andy uses Jessica's words to proclaim Erin IS relationship material — turning the insult into a declaration in front of Jessica
jokes.explanation: Good callback structure. Andy weaponizing Jessica's language ('total relationship material') in a declaration of love in front of her is poetically satisfying and slightly oblivious — exactly how Andy would do it.

jokes.text: Jessica's friends' escalating reactions: 'Why the hell did you come back here? / Go away / Get lost / Get out / You ruined my party / Who does that? / Yeah, run away. Run away. / You're disgusting / I can't believe you're not gay / Get out of here / Don't come back'
jokes.setup: Andy has returned to the bachelorette party to declare his love for Erin, having just broken up with Jessica and claiming to be gay
jokes.punchline: The group reacts with an escalating barrage of overlapping insults, with 'I can't believe you're not gay' being the standout line
jokes.explanation: Good escalation set piece. The barrage of insults works as a comedic wall of sound, but 'I can't believe you're not gay' — from Kenny, who Andy convinced by citing John Stamos — is the standout joke within the sequence. It recontextualizes Kenny's investment in the gay claim as weirdly personal.

jokes.text: Hank the security guard: 'I thought I was very specific about you not letting up a magician.' / 'Yes, ma'am. I got my eyes open.' / 'He came and went.' / 'What? That ain't right.'
jokes.setup: Pam confronts Hank about the magician getting into the building despite being told not to
jokes.punchline: Hank's response — 'I got my eyes open' — implies active surveillance; he then has no explanation for the failure
jokes.explanation: Mild Hank bit. 'That ain't right' as a sincere but baffled response to security failure is mildly funny. Hank's character consistency (cheerful incompetence) is here but the joke doesn't escalate to anything exceptional.

jokes.text: "Wait a minute. You said it was a magician, right? You don't think he could have used... It couldn't have been... Let's just go."
jokes.setup: Hank is trying to explain how the magician got past security
jokes.punchline: Hank's train of thought leads him to genuinely wonder if the magician used magic to get in — then thinks better of it and drops it with 'Let's just go'
jokes.explanation: Excellent closing joke. The episode ends on Hank genuinely entertaining the possibility that the magician used actual magic — then dismissing it without conclusion ('Let's just go'). The truncated thought, the brief openness to magic as an explanation, and the immediate retreat are all perfectly executed. 'It couldn't have been...' leaving the sentence open is funnier than any completion. Great economy and a satisfying absurdist button for the episode.

tmdb_overview: Robert California forces the office to throw a welcome party for Nellie, but the Party Planning Committee works on ways to sabotage it. Meanwhile, Erin tries to help Andy figure out a way to break up with Jessica.
